rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Only the first pair needs improvement, while all other pairs have substantial resolution margins. Raising temperature tests selectivity for this pair and should shorten retention, preserving the zero time penalty.
Injection 2 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method, checking whether the first pair remains at R ≥ 1.5.

Narrowing the gradient window makes the slope intermediate between injections 2 and 3, aiming to restore first-pair resolution above 1.5 while remaining faster than injection 2. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction.

Shift the starting fraction upward while keeping the slope close to injection 4 to remove low-organic time and seek faster separation. This tests whether the first pair retains full resolution; the endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Test the low-temperature selectivity limit using injection 4’s gradient, since a change in elution order could provide another route to resolving the first pair. Injection 4 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark if this cooler run loses resolution or incurs a time penalty.

The cool run resolved the first pair but exposed a late three-peak cluster. A substantially steeper gradient tests whether that cluster separates through slope-dependent selectivity while bringing the last peak below 10 minutes.

The late cluster barely responded to slope, so test a 5 °C temperature increase from injection 6 to change its selectivity. The shallower gradient should preserve the early pair’s resolution, while warming should bring the last peak below 10 minutes.

Return to the successful high-temperature region with a slope just slightly steeper than injection 4. This should shorten retention while keeping the critical first pair near or above R = 1.5; the endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 9 to test the fastest gradient likely to retain first-pair resolution of 1.5. The last peak may enter the final hold, so this run also tests whether the lower endpoint still permits a shorter fully resolved separation.

Test a higher starting fraction with a slightly shallower slope to see whether selectivity can offset early-peak compression and shorten the separation. Injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Test an intermediate-temperature route with a higher starting fraction to shorten retention and alter early-pair selectivity. At 35 °C, the late cluster may separate better than at 30 °C while the first pair may retain the cooler-temperature elution order.

Test whether a higher starting fraction changes the first pair’s selectivity enough to resolve it at 35 °C, using a shallower slope to limit compression. This could shorten the cooler-temperature separation, though early retention is the main risk.

Return to 60 °C and compensate for the raised starting fraction with a shallower gradient than injection 5. This targets full first-pair resolution with a last-peak time near the fastest successful methods.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 10 while keeping the last peak inside the gradient. This probes the speed limit near R = 1.5 for the first pair; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a cooler fully resolved alternative with a low starting fraction and shallower slope to protect the first pair. At 35 °C the late cluster should have better selectivity than at 30 °C, with the last peak expected near but below 10 minutes.

Slightly flatten the gradient to lift the first pair above R = 1.5, while raising the endpoint to prevent the prolonged final hold seen in injection 16. This tests a fully resolved lower-temperature alternative; injection 10 remains the fastest maximum-score method.

Refine injection 14 with a slightly steeper slope, targeting first-pair resolution just above 1.5 and a modestly shorter elution time. The high endpoint keeps the last peak inside the gradient; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

The fastest successful methods sit close to the first-pair resolution threshold. Slightly flatten injection 4’s gradient to gain resolution margin while keeping all peaks inside the gradient and the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient to increase the first pair’s resolution margin while targeting a last-peak time below 10 minutes. Monitor the third-to-fourth pair, whose resolution has declined as the gradient becomes shallower; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Steepen injection 20 by one endpoint step to shorten elution while retaining more resolution margin than the fastest methods. The first and third-to-fourth pairs should both remain above 1.5, preserving the maximum CRF.

Raise the starting fraction and slightly flatten the slope relative to injection 21 to shorten retention while protecting the first pair. This targets a faster maximum-score method with more resolution margin than injection 10.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 22 to shorten retention while using some of its first-pair resolution margin. The resulting slope is slightly shallower than injection 14’s successful slope, so full resolution is expected.

Use a slope between injections 19 and 21 to retain a useful first-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. This targets another maximum-score method; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Trim injection 24’s gradient duration and endpoint while keeping a similar slope, targeting full resolution and elution within 10 minutes. The campaign has already reached the maximum CRF; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
